POSITIVE SCALAR CURVATURE ON NONCOMPACT MANIFOLDS
AND THE LIOUVILLE THEOREM
MARTIN LESOURD, RYAN UNGER, AND SHING-TUNG YAU
Abstract. Using minimal hypersurfaces, we obtain topological obstructions to ad-
mitting complete metrics with positive scalar curvature R > 0 on a given class of
non-compact manifolds M n for n < 8.
We show that the Liouville theorem for locally conformally ﬂat manifolds M n with
R ≥0 follows from the impossibility of admitting a complete metric with R > 0 on
T n#M n. With the recent work of Chodosh-Li, the Liouville theorem is now proved
in all remaining cases.
Finally, using MOTS instead of minimal hypersurfaces, we show an Initial Data
Set version of these results with the Dominant Energy Scalar µ−|J| appearing instead
of R.
1. Main results
All manifolds are assumed smooth and orientable. A classic result of Schoen–Yau
[30] for n ≤7 and Gromov–Lawson [18, 19] for all n states that the n-torus T n does
not admit a Riemannian metric with positive scalar curvature R > 0.
Theorem 1.1 (Geroch’s Conjecture). T n does not admit a metric with R > 0.
Interest in T n originally came from the Positive Mass Theorem [29] in General Rel-
ativity, which states that an asymptotically ﬂat manifold with R ≥0 has non-negative
ADM mass and zero if and only if the manifold is ﬂat.1 Although not originally ap-
proached in this way, a compactiﬁcation argument of Lokhamp [24] showed that the
Positive Mass Theorem follows from the non-existence of a smooth complete metric
with R > 0 on compact manifolds of the form T n # Xn.
Here, letting Xn be non-compact and replacing T n with the class of Cn manifolds2,
we show the following.
Theorem 1.2. Manifolds of the form Mn = Cn # Xn do not admit a complete smooth
metric with R > 0 if either
(i) n = 3,
(ii) or 4 ≤n ≤7 and Mn is (λ, ρ)-contractible.
and moreover any complete smooth metric with R ≥0 is Ricci-ﬂat.

2. Proof of Theorem 1.2
2.1. Warm-up. Recall the following very classical result.
Proposition 2.1. The torus T 2 does not admit a metric of positive scalar curvature.
This can easily be proved using the Gauss–Bonnet theorem.
However, following
Synge and Cartan, we can argue as follows. The torus contains a nontrivial free homo-
topy class of curves L. Using the Arzela–Ascoli theorem and basic results on geodesics,
we may ﬁnd a closed geodesic γ ∈L of minimal length. The second variation formula
implies this geodesic is unstable because of positive curvature, which is a contradiction.
This technique motivated the minimal hypersurface approach to scalar curvature.
The compactness of the torus is used in two places. Firstly, to apply the Arzela–
Ascoli theorem to maps S1 →T 2 and secondly, to ensure the positivity of the convexity
radius of (T 2, g). However, the Cartan–Synge argument goes through if we know that
the “relevant” curves all lie in some large ball.
Theorem 2.2. Let X2 be any surface without boundary. Then T 2#X2 does not admit
a complete metric of positive scalar curvature.
Proof. Consider a free homotopy class L corresponding to going once around one of
the circular factors in T 2. Let C ⊂T 2#X2 be a “surgery circle” associated to the
connected sum. Then C /∈L. In T 2, C bounds an open disk. Call the complement of
this disk K ⊂X2 # T 2.
Let {γi} ⊂L be a length-minimizing sequence of smooth curves. For each i, γi∩K ̸=
∅for otherwise γi would be nullhomotopic in T 2, contradicting the choice of L. Let
ℓ= supi L(γi) < ∞. Then by the triangle inequality, γi is eventually contained in the
2ℓ-neighborhood of K. Since g is complete, this neighborhood is relatively compact.
Now a subsequence of {γi} tends to a closed length-minimizing geodesic which can
be shown to be unstable, and we have a contradiction.
□
The topology of X2 # T 2 prevents the minimizing sequence from “escaping oﬀto
inﬁnity” – the compact set K anchors L. In fact, the completeness of g prevented
the curves from entering the noncompact end at all. This is much stronger than what
can be expected for minimal hypersurfaces and in general we will have degeneration of
topology at inﬁnity.

Remark 2.9. If Mn is compact, then Cn is equivalent to C′n for n = 3 and n ≥5.
Indeed, Cn =⇒C′n in all dimensions since a map f : M →T n−2 is given by n −2

We can also see that C′n =⇒Cn when n ̸= 4. When n ≥5, this is because a map

However, since the sphere theorem fails for 4-manifolds (desingularizing a double

Abstract: Using minimal hypersurfaces, we obtain topological obstructions to ad- mitting complete metrics with positive scalar curvature R > 0 on a given class of non-compact manifolds M n for n < 8. We show that the Liouville theorem for locally conformally ﬂat manifolds M n with R ≥0 follows from the impossibility of admitting a complete metric with R > 0 on T n#M n. With the recent work of Chodosh-Li, the Liouville theorem is now proved in all remaining cases. Finally, using MOTS instead of minimal hypersurfaces, we show an Initial Data Set version of these results with the Dominant Energy Scalar µ−|J| appearing instead of R.
